title: Who Needs a Starting QB? Not Seattle or Minnesota.
subtitle: The Seahawks and Vikings are showing how to build a quarterback-proof contender — and even Kansas City is taking notes.
contentHtml:
Losing your starting quarterback is supposed to be the easiest way to ruin an NFL season. Unless, apparently, you are the Seattle Seahawks or Minnesota Vikings — who both moved to 2-0 on Sunday with backups under center. (Drew Lock for Seattle in place of an injured Sam Darnold, Carson Wentz for Minnesota in place of Kyler Murray.)

Subscribe now

It hasn’t always been pretty, of course. Lock and the Seahawks offense struggled to move the ball for much of the opener against New England, though he’s gotten progressively better ever since (playing Arizona might help with that). Wentz has been more uneven, but even at his worst he still occupies that gray area between league-average and the replacement level. They’re the types of quarterbacks who can grind out wins by scores like 13-10 and 9-3 — provided they have the right team around them. And few backup QBs could be on more perfect teams for this assignment than these two.

One major thing both Seattle and Minnesota have in common is that their paths to victory don’t run exclusively through the quarterback, and they haven’t for a while. In the modern, pass-happy NFL, that might sound like a bad thing; teams will often move heaven and earth in order to acquire a franchise QB in the draft or via other means.

But Seattle won the Super Bowl last season primarily on the strength of its defense, with an offense that was fairly unremarkable — both in its overall efficiency (No. 16 in Expected Points Added per game) and its reliance on passing relative to rushing (they also ranked 16th with 64.9 percent of total yards coming via the pass). And Vikings D coordinator Brian Flores has continued to earn his reputation as one of the game’s best defensive tacticians, giving Minnesota a chance to win each week no matter who they have starting at quarterback.

As it turns out, that combination — a strong defense + no particular over-reliance on the passing game offensively — is somewhat rare among contending teams. Looking at all NFL squads with a positive point differential since the start of 2025, the only two who check in as allowing fewer than 19 PPG on defense and rely on passing for less than 65 percent of their total yardage are… the Vikings and Seahawks.

So if any two teams could afford to lose their starting QBs, these might be the two to do it. That’s no knock on any of the signal-callers involved, either, but more a statement on the strength of the team around them.

In fairness to Seattle’s passers in particular, Darnold had a career-year last regular season and was even better in the playoffs,1 while Lock is absolutely holding his own on the EPA ledger to start this season. But it’s also true that throwing to Jaxon Smith-Njigba, with defensive support from the likes of Ernest Jones, DeMarcus Lawrence, Byron Murphy, Leonard Williams and Devon Witherspoon, helps put a quarterback in position to succeed.

Minnesota, for its part, has gotten substantially less from its QBs over the past two seasons, with a cumulative total of -128.3 EPA above average since the start of 2025, though almost all of that (-120.0) came from two names — J.J. McCarthy and Max Brosmer. Wentz has been a -5.6 in 6 starts during that span, much closer to league-average. Plus, ESPN reported that Murray was cleared to return from his concussion next week anyway.

And if there is a real trend toward being at least a little less dependent on the quarterback, another early-season candidate moving in that direction is an unlikely one indeed.

The Kansas City Chiefs are also 2-0, and relying on the running game — with new acquisition Kenneth Walker III — more than ever. At no other point in the Patrick Mahomes Era (since 2018) had K.C. gotten less than 60 percent of its total yards via passing until right now, as the aerial attack sits at just 59.3 percent. Relatedly, Walker has accounted for 39.3 percent of all K.C.’s offensive yards, which is the most by a Chiefs running back in a decade and the second-most since the heyday of Larry Johnson.

Walker is carrying a surprising load for Kansas City

Is it any coincidence that Walker was also Seattle’s lead back last season — especially in the playoffs — en route to winning Super Bowl MVP honors, becoming the first RB to earn that honor since Terrell Davis in 1997? Probably not. You want insurance for Mahomes as he returns from knee surgery? Go get the guy who just helped a less QB-dependent squad win the Super Bowl.

After a cruel day for quarterback injuries, two other teams who may wish they had more in the way of such insurance are the Chicago Bears (who lost the electric Caleb Williams to a scary-seeming hamstring injury) and the Washington Commanders (whose own young QB, Jayden Daniels, dislocated his non-throwing elbow for the second time in as many years). Tack on another from Monday Night, too, with Jaxson Dart of the Giants going down early with a leg injury.

The teams are not totally bereft of supporting talent — or coaching talent, for that matter, with Ben Johnson, Dan Quinn and John Harbaugh — but at the same time, Chicago ranked 23rd in points allowed last year, New York ranked 26th and Washington ranked 27th. That’s basically the opposite of the Seattle/Minnesota formula. And don’t even get started on the 0-2 Atlanta Falcons, who’ve burned through QB1 and QB2 already, then benched QB3 Cooper Rush for his own horribleness in Sunday’s ugly 34-3 loss to Carolina.

No amount of insurance could have saved Atlanta from Rush’s 5 turnovers in 1.5 games of action thus far. And don’t get me wrong: a real franchise quarterback remains the most valuable thing to have in football. But Seattle and Minnesota are proving that the best backup plan isn’t actually another quarterback — it’s a supporting cast good enough to keep winning without one.
